3.text: **The behavior of dicarboxylic acids on heating** depends on their structure: oxalic and malonic acids **decarboxylate** on heating (HOOC−CH~2~−COOH → CH~3~COOH + CO~2~), while succinic and glutaric acids lose water to form five- and six-membered **cyclic anhydrides**. Biological decarboxylation (of pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate) is also made easier by a carbonyl or carboxyl group next to the carboxyl group.

parts.text: Foods rich in **oxalate** are sorrel, spinach, rhubarb, cocoa and tea. Normally calcium binds oxalate in the intestinal lumen; when fats are poorly absorbed (intestinal diseases), calcium binds to fatty acids instead, much free oxalate is absorbed, and **enteric hyperoxaluria** and kidney stones develop.

6.text: Structure and action: salicylates and sulfonamides

**Aspirin** transfers an acetyl group to the serine hydroxyl in the active site of cyclooxygenase (COX) — the enzyme is **irreversibly** inactivated. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot synthesize new enzyme, so a single small dose (75–100 mg) stops **thromboxane** synthesis for the whole life of the platelet (≈ 7–10 days) — the prevention of cardiovascular disease is based on this.

**Sulfonamides and trimethoprim** block two successive steps of folate synthesis: a sulfonamide, as a competitor of PABA, blocks dihydropteroate synthase, and trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase. Together (co-trimoxazole) they act **synergistically**. Humans obtain folate from food and do not have this enzyme — this is the basis of the drugs’ selective action.

parts.text: **Aspirin is not given** to children under 16 during a viral infection (influenza, chickenpox) — it can cause **Reye syndrome** (acute liver failure and cerebral edema). In children, paracetamol or ibuprofen is used to lower fever.

blocks.text: **Biogenic amines** are formed by the **decarboxylation** of amino acids: R−CH(NH~2~)−COOH → R−CH~2~−NH~2~ + CO~2~. The reaction is catalyzed by decarboxylases that depend on pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B~6~). Biogenic amines have strong physiological effects at low concentrations — they are neurotransmitters, hormones and local regulators.

blocks.text: The action of biogenic amines must be stopped quickly. They are oxidatively deaminated by **monoamine oxidase** (MAO) (R−CH~2~−NH~2~ → R−CHO + NH~3~), and catecholamines are in addition methylated by **catechol-O-methyltransferase** (COMT). The aldehydes formed are oxidized to acids and excreted in the urine (vanillylmandelic acid is the main catecholamine metabolite).

parts.text: **The “cheese reaction”:** if a patient taking MAO inhibitors (some antidepressants) eats tyramine-rich food (aged cheese, smoked meat, wine, soy sauce), tyramine is not broken down in the intestine and liver. It displaces noradrenaline from nerve endings — a **hypertensive crisis** develops. That is why such patients are advised to follow a special diet.

blocks.text: **Ketone bodies** are three substances formed in the liver from acetyl-CoA: **acetoacetate** (a β-keto acid), **β-hydroxybutyrate** (a β-hydroxy acid) and **acetone** (a product of the spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate). In starvation, a carbohydrate-free diet and insulin deficiency, fatty acids are oxidized intensively, acetyl-CoA is not fully used in the Krebs cycle and is converted into ketone bodies.

items: The liver **does not use** ketone bodies (it lacks the enzyme that activates them) — it releases them into the blood.
The heart and skeletal muscles, the renal cortex and, in prolonged starvation, the **brain** use ketone bodies as an energy source.
Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are strong acids (pK~a~ 3.6 and 4.7): when produced in large amounts they consume the bicarbonate buffer and cause **ketoacidosis**.
Acetone is volatile and hardly metabolized — it is exhaled through the lungs, and the breath smells of **“rotten apples”**.

blocks.text: **Keto–enol tautomerism:** acetoacetate and its esters exist in equilibrium between the keto and enol forms: CH~3~−CO−CH~2~−COOR ⇄ CH~3~−C(OH)=CH−COOR. The enol form gives a violet color with FeCl~3~. In urine, ketone bodies are detected by the red-violet color formed with **sodium nitroprusside** in an alkaline medium (Legal’s test, test strips).

skills.title: Skill: detecting ketone bodies in urine (Legal’s test)

items: Pour 1–2 mL of urine into a test tube.
Add 2–3 drops of freshly prepared 5 % sodium nitroprusside solution and 0.5 mL of 10 % NaOH — a red color appears.
Add a few drops of glacial acetic acid: the red color due to creatinine disappears, while if ketone bodies are present a **red-violet** color persists and intensifies.
Grade the result with “+” signs or compare the test-strip color with the scale.
Interpret a positive result together with the patient’s glucose level and clinical condition.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: A teenager with type 1 diabetes mellitus missed his insulin injections. He has nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and deep, noisy breathing; his breath smells fruity. Glucose 24 mmol/L, blood β-hydroxybutyrate 5.2 mmol/L.
cases.ask: Why have the ketone bodies increased? How do they cause acidosis? What is the smell of the breath due to?
cases.answer: Without insulin, cells cannot use glucose and lipolysis increases in adipose tissue; β-oxidation of fatty acids in the liver produces much **acetyl-CoA**, which is converted into ketone bodies. β-Hydroxybutyrate 5.2 mmol/L (> 3) — **diabetic ketoacidosis**. Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are strong organic acids; they release H^+^, consume the bicarbonate buffer and cause metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. The deep Kussmaul breathing is respiratory compensation. **Acetone**, formed by the decarboxylation of acetoacetate, is volatile and is exhaled.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: A woman taking an MAO inhibitor for depression ate aged cheese and drank red wine at a party. An hour later she had a severe headache and palpitations, and her blood pressure was 220/120 mm Hg.
cases.ask: Explain the biochemical mechanism of the hypertensive crisis.
cases.answer: Cheese and wine contain much **tyramine** — the decarboxylation product of tyrosine. Normally tyramine is broken down by **MAO** in the intestinal wall and liver. When MAO is blocked, tyramine enters the blood and displaces **noradrenaline** from sympathetic nerve endings; since noradrenaline is also not broken down by MAO, its effect is enhanced — vessels constrict and blood pressure rises sharply. This is called the “cheese reaction”; the patient should have been warned in advance to avoid tyramine-containing foods.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: Several customers who ate canned tuna at a restaurant developed flushing of the face and neck, headache, a burning sensation in the mouth and itching 20–30 minutes later. None of them had a history of allergy.
cases.ask: What is the chemical cause of the condition? How is it treated?
cases.answer: This is **scombroid poisoning**: in improperly stored fish, **histidine** is converted into **histamine** by bacterial decarboxylase. Histamine is not destroyed by cooking; eaten in large amounts it causes an allergy-like reaction (vasodilation, flushing, itching), but without an immune mechanism. Treatment is with **antihistamines** (H~1~ blockers, and H~2~ blockers if needed); severe cases are treated like an allergic reaction.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A patient with a urinary tract infection was prescribed co-trimoxazole (sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim).
cases.ask: What is the biochemical basis for giving the two drugs together? Why do they hardly affect human cells?
cases.answer: Bacteria synthesize folic acid themselves. **Sulfamethoxazole** is a structural analog of PABA: it competitively takes the place of PABA at dihydropteroate synthase. **Trimethoprim** blocks the bacterial dihydrofolate reductase at the next step. Because two successive steps of one pathway are blocked, the effect is **synergistic** and bactericidal, and resistance develops slowly. Humans take folate ready-made from food (they have no dihydropteroate synthase), and trimethoprim acts on human reductase 50 000 times more weakly — this is the basis of the selective action.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A patient with Parkinson disease has been found to lack dopamine, but for treatment levodopa together with carbidopa was prescribed instead of dopamine itself.
cases.ask: Why is dopamine itself not given? What role does carbidopa play?
cases.answer: Dopamine is a polar amine that is positively charged at physiological pH; it **does not cross the blood–brain barrier**. Levodopa (L-DOPA) is an amino acid that enters the brain via the neutral amino acid transporter and is converted there into **dopamine** by DOPA decarboxylase. However, much of the levodopa is decarboxylated in the periphery before it reaches the brain, causing nausea and arrhythmias. **Carbidopa** blocks peripheral decarboxylase but does not itself enter the brain — the fraction of levodopa reaching the brain increases, and the dose can be reduced.

cards.back: Decarboxylation products of amino acids: histamine, serotonin, GABA, dopamine; coenzyme — B~6~
Monoamine oxidase — oxidatively deaminates biogenic amines; with its inhibitors — the “cheese reaction”
Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone; formed in the liver, increased in insulin deficiency
Ketone bodies in urine give a red-violet color with sodium nitroprusside
Irreversibly acetylates COX; antiplatelet effect for the life of the platelet
Sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim — block two steps of folate synthesis and act synergistically
